methods.text: The mental model is Charles Xavier's Cerebro: cerebellum maps which neurons matter, the `.cblm` pack is the *amplifier* that pre-seeds the model toward a specific behavior — coding, math, roleplay, format-strict, refusal-stripped — by writing into the exact bytes our ablation dat
A `.cblm` is not a LoRA adapter and not a separate model. It's a **targeted patch** against ablation-identified slots in a base GGUF, plus optional pre-computed runtime state.
Cerebellum's ablation identifies tensors where crushing to Q2_K either improves the model (demote candidates) or causes negligible loss. Those tensors can be replaced with task-specialized versions:
| `cblm-train` | Fine-tune ONLY ablation-identified dead tensors (frozen-base partial finetune) | Phase 2 |

- **Targeting strategy.** LoRA targets are heuristic (typically `q_proj`, `v_proj`); `.cblm` LoRA targets are the demote candidates ablation has *proven* are safe to modify on a per-objective basis. No one else has this data.

- **Frozen-base partial fine-tune.** `cblm-train` only updates ablation-identified dead tensors. Not a new training algorithm — just a constrained training scope that no one else can specify because no one else has the ablation data.
- **RAG quality depends on retrieval quality.** `.cblm` quality depends on how well the ablation identified safe slots and how well the pack was trained.
| 1. Finish v2 ablation, identify dead slots with confidence | now → ~6h | Per-tensor sensitivity ranking |
| 5. Bench cerebellum-base + code.cblm vs cerebellum-base alone vs uniform Q3_K_S | days | Validation against gates |
- **Quantization saturation:** baking a LoRA into a Q2_K dead slot may saturate (low precision can't represent fine deltas). May need to lift the slot to Q4 first, then merge. Test required.
| **Mergekit** (Charles Goddard) | Slerp/ties/dare merging of full models | Operates on whole models, not targeted slots. We target by ablation. |
The cerebellum contribution is the **targeting strategy** (ablation-informed) and the **bundle convention** (three existing formats + manifest = one downloadable pack). Both are small but real.

`.cblm` is a small bundle wrapping three existing llama.cpp primitives (GGUF LoRA, control vectors, runtime state) with a manifest, targeting ablation-identified dead-weight slots in a base GGUF — distributed as a single file, mergeable via ~200 lines of Python, runnable in any s
This is what LoRA-on-the-Hub *should* have been but wasn't — because no one had ablation data to target with.

name: Cerebellum project mission and north star

**Why:** This is who Cerebellum is FOR. The user runs a 3090 (24 GB but realistic users target 8-12 GB). When Q4_K_M doesn't fit and Q3_K_S is meaningfully worse than the model could be, that's the gap Cerebellum exists to fill. Every published build has to actually serve someone on a constrained card — otherwise it's noise, not progress.

- **Every feature decision filters through "does this serve smaller-without-being-dumber for resource-constrained users?"** Multi-domain ablation does (preserves code ability under tight budget). Adding a 13B-class quant doesn't (audience is people who can't fit those). Adding fancy compression that requires custom inference does NOT serve the goal — Cerebel
- **Resist scope creep upward.** It's tempting to chase 70B builds because they look impressive. Stay anchored to the people on 8-12 GB cards. They're who Cerebellum was built for.

- **Resist features that look smart but don't help the audience.** A custom inference runtime, a research-grade lossless compression scheme, a non-llama.cpp dependency — all of these would technically improve compression numbers but shrink the audience to zero. Stock llama.cpp + standard GGUF + stock inference is non-negotiable.

Cerebellum measures which weight groups survive extreme compression and which don't, then writes a single GGUF with per-tensor precision assignments. v3 uses 360 tensor-level overrides guided by group ablation and reverse ablation analysis.
| Benchmark | **v3 (11 GB)** | v1 (12 GB) | Q3_K_M (15.6 GB) |

v3 at 11 GB is **29% smaller** than stock Q3_K_M (15.6 GB) while outperforming it on 5 of 6 benchmarks. The Q2_K regularization effect on gate/mixing weights actively improves downstream task performance despite reducing perplexity.
| `attn_qkv` | Q3_K_M | Critical for vision and attention routing |
| `ssm_out` | Q3_K_M | Most sensitive tensor per ablation (+0.24 PPL) |
| `ffn_down_exps` | Q2_K | Acceptable loss for size savings |
Full ablation methodology and results are in the `ablation/` directory:
- `group_ablation_results.log` — Forward ablation: demote each group to Q2_K, measure PPL
- `reverse_ablation_results.log` — Reverse ablation: from fully-demoted v1, restore each group
Key finding from reverse ablation: **6 of 10 groups perform better at Q2_K than Q3_K_M** — imatrix-guided Q2_K acts as beneficial regularization on gate, mixing, and shared expert weights.
| `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Cerebellum-v3.gguf` | 11 GB | v3 — recommended, 29% smaller than Q3_K_M |
